title: Conditions for Quantum Advantage in AC Power Flow
authors: Parikshit Pareek, Abhijith Jayakumar, Carleton Coffrin, Sidhant Misra
abstract: This paper aims to contextualize the requirements for Quantum Computing (QC) algorithms to achieve a quantum advantage in solving the alternating current power flow (ACPF) problem, with a focus on runtime complexity. First, we establish a benchmark for a QC iterative solver to demonstrate an advantage over the classical Newton-Raphson Load Flow (NRLF) algorithm. Next, we derive a baseline expression for the end-to-end runtime complexity of any Gate-based QC algorithm as $Ω(N κ/\varepsilon),$ reflecting dependence on system size $N$, condition number $κ$, and error tolerance $\varepsilon$. Finally, we highlight key areas where QC algorithms may offer potential benefits over NRLF in addressing the standard ACPF problem.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes whether Quantum Computing can solve the Alternating Current Power Flow (ACPF) problem faster than classical methods. It derives complexity bounds for both quantum and classical solvers, concluding that while a lower bound exists for QC, practical quantum advantage is unlikely due to unfavorable scaling with required error tolerance.
main_problem: The paper investigates the theoretical conditions under which Quantum Computing (QC) algorithms can achieve a demonstrable quantum advantage over classical methods when solving the Alternating Current Power Flow (ACPF) problem.
main_result: The analysis establishes an optimistic lower bound for any Quantum-ACPF solver as $\Omega(N\kappa/\epsilon)$, but subsequent comparison with classical complexity suggests that achieving a practical quantum advantage is highly challenging due to the $1/\epsilon$ dependence.
method: The authors perform rigorous complexity benchmarking by deriving baseline runtime expressions for both classical (Newton-Raphson Load Flow) and theoretical gate-based QC solvers, comparing their scaling with system size ($N$), condition number ($\kappa$), and error tolerance ($\epsilon$).
model_or_system: The physical model is the electrical energy system analyzed via the nonlinear ACPF equations. The computational task involves iteratively solving linear systems derived from the Jacobian matrix of this power flow problem.
key_observables: Quantum/Classical runtime complexity, Quantum-to-Classical cost ratio ($Q/C$), and the condition number ($\kappa$) of the Jacobian matrix.
important_parameters: System size $N$, Condition Number $\kappa$, Error Tolerance $\epsilon$ (measured in $\ell_2$-norm).
main_assumptions: The quantum complexity analysis optimistically assumes access to Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) and that the total time is dominated by a lower bound of $\Omega(N\kappa/\epsilon)$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows variations in the Jacobian condition number ($\kappa$) across different datasets. Figure 2 compares the complexity bounds: top panel shows the classical NRLF bound, while the bottom panel illustrates the derived quantum lower bound.
paper_structure: The paper first benchmarks QC solvers against the classical NRLF algorithm. It then derives a general baseline runtime complexity for gate-based QC algorithms ($\Omega(N\kappa/\epsilon)$). Finally, it compares this theoretical quantum cost to the established classical benchmark to determine feasibility of advantage.
why_interesting: While the application is in power systems (not core condensed matter physics), the rigorous comparative analysis of algorithmic scaling ($O(\cdot)$ vs $\Omega(\cdot)$) based on system parameters ($\kappa, N, \epsilon$) provides a valuable theoretical framework for assessing quantum computational feasibility across diverse scientific domains.
